unit.title: Money and inflation
unit.description: What money is, why it loses value and how it grows with compound interest

steps.title: What money is for
steps.body:
Money does three jobs:

• **Means of payment:** you swap work for bread without having to barter.
• **Unit of account:** you know a coffee is worth less than a bike.
• **Store of value:** you can keep it for tomorrow… although, as we'll see, it slowly wears away.

steps.title: Four words people mix up
steps.body:
• **Income:** what comes in (salary, allowance, rent you collect). It's a flow: it arrives every month.
• **Savings:** the part of your income you don't spend.
• **Net worth:** what you own minus what you owe. It's a snapshot at one moment.
• **Investment:** putting your savings to work so they produce more.
steps.tip: Earning a lot isn't the same as having a lot: what counts is what you keep.

steps.title: The snapshot and the film
steps.body: Your net worth is the snapshot: €3,000 in the bank + a €6,000 car − €4,000 left on the car loan = €5,000. Your income and savings are the film: how that snapshot changes every month.
steps.key: Wealth is net worth, not salary: what you own minus what you owe.

steps.title: What inflation is
steps.body:
Inflation is the **general rise in prices**. If bread, electricity and rent go up by 3 % on average in a year, inflation has been 3 %.

In Spain it's measured by the INE (the national statistics office) with the **CPI**. In 2025 it averaged 2.7 %.

steps.title: Play with inflation
steps.body: Move the sliders: how much will your euros buy in a few years' time?
steps.tip: Trick: 70 ÷ inflation = years until your money buys half as much.

steps.title: Why prices go up
steps.body: They rise when there's more money or more demand than things to buy, or when producing costs more (energy in 2022). The ECB tries to keep inflation around **2 %** in the medium term by raising or cutting interest rates.
steps.key: With inflation, money that sits still buys a little less every year.

u1l3.title: The CPI and your shopping basket

steps.title: How it's measured
steps.body:
Every month the INE tracks the prices of a **basket** of hundreds of goods and services (food, housing, transport, leisure…). The **CPI** is the change in that basket compared with the year before.

Each item is weighted by what households spend on it on average.

steps.title: Headline and core
steps.body:
• **Headline CPI:** the whole basket.
• **Core inflation:** leaves out unprocessed food and energy, which swing up and down a lot. It shows the underlying trend.

If electricity shoots up one month, headline jumps a lot but core barely moves.

steps.title: Your personal inflation
steps.body: The CPI is an average. If you spend a lot on rent and transport, your inflation may be higher than the official figure; if you hardly drive, lower.
steps.key: The CPI is everyone's average: your inflation depends on what you spend on.

steps.title: Real return
steps.body:
To avoid losing purchasing power, your money has to earn more than inflation.

**Real return ≈ return − inflation.**

An account paying 2 % with 2.7 % inflation makes you lose 0.7 % a year.

steps.title: How much idle savings lose
steps.body: Put €10,000 away for 10 years with 2.5 % inflation and see how much is lost by doing nothing.
steps.tip: Just because the number in your account doesn't go down doesn't mean you're not losing.

steps.title: Safe isn't the same as protected
steps.body: Deposits are covered up to €100,000 by the Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (Spain's deposit guarantee scheme): you don't lose euros. But you can lose **purchasing power** if they earn less than inflation.
steps.key: What matters isn't how many euros you have, but what you can buy with them.

steps.title: Simple and compound
steps.body:
**Simple:** you always earn on what you put in. €1,000 at 7 % gives €70 a year: after 30 years, €3,100.

**Compound:** you earn on what you put in plus what you've already earned. That €1,000 turns into **€7,612**.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Start with €0 and add €100 a month for 30 years at 7 %: you put in €36,000 and end up with about €122,000. Try starting 10 years earlier.
steps.tip: These are examples, not promises: the stock market doesn't give 7 % every year.

steps.title: Ana and Bruno
steps.body: Both put in €200 a month at 7 % until they're 65. Ana starts at 25 and reaches **€524,963**; Bruno starts at 35 and reaches **€243,994**. Ana puts in only €24,000 more and ends up with more than double. And watch out: it also works against you with expensive debt.
steps.key: Gains generate new gains: the sooner you start, the more time works for you.

steps.title: The trick
steps.body:
How many years does it take your money to double? Divide **72 by the annual return**.

• At 6 % → 72 ÷ 6 = **12 years**.
• At 9 % → **8 years**.
• At 2 % → **36 years**.

It's a very good approximation between 4 % and 12 %.

steps.title: Check it
steps.body: Move the return and compare the rule of 72 with the exact calculation.
steps.tip: It also works the other way round: with 6 % inflation, prices double in about 12 years.

steps.title: What it's for
steps.body: It lets you compare in your head. A fund that charges 2 % a year cuts your return from 7 % to 5 %: you go from doubling in ~10 years to doubling in ~14.
steps.key: 72 ÷ return = years to double. It works for gains, inflation and debt.

u1l1-1.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
u1l1-1.explanation: Income and savings are flows (every month); net worth is a snapshot at one moment.
right: What you don't spend of what comes in
What you own minus what you owe
Putting savings to work to produce more

u1l1-2.prompt: You have €2,500 in the bank and a laptop worth €800, and you owe €1,200 on a loan. What's your net worth?
u1l1-2.explanation: 2,500 + 800 − 1,200 = €2,100. Net worth subtracts what you owe.

u1l1-3.prompt: Which of these functions of money breaks down when inflation is high?
options: Unit of account to compare a coffee and a bike
u1l1-3.explanation: With high inflation, money you keep buys less every year: it stops being a good store of value.

u1l1-4.prompt: Someone who earns €4,000 a month and spends it all can have a lower net worth than someone who earns €1,500 and saves €300.
u1l1-4.explanation: Net worth grows with what you save and invest, not with what you earn.

u1l1-5.prompt: Is it income or net worth?
options: The rent you collect every month
u1l1-5.explanation: Income is what comes in; net worth is what you build up.

options: I'll spend it all, I deserve it
I'll take out a loan for a pricier car
I'll set some aside every month before spending
u1l1-6.explanation: A pay rise doesn't make you richer if your spending rises just as much: what makes you richer is what you set aside.
feedback: Enjoying it is fine, but if spending swallows all of it, your net worth doesn't budge.
That way the rise goes on repayments and your net worth could fall.
That's it! Set aside €100 a month and in a year that's €1,200 more net worth.
lines: I've just had a €300 a month pay rise 🎉
What should I do with it?

u1l1-7.prompt: Net worth = what you own − what you ____.
u1l1-7.explanation: Debts subtract: a €15,000 car with a €12,000 loan only adds €3,000 to you.

u1l1-8.explanation: It's income: a flow that comes in every month. What you build up with it is net worth.

u1l1-9.prompt: Marta earns €1,800 and spends €1,750. Pablo earns €1,300 and spends €1,000. In 5 years, without investing anything, who'll have saved more?
options: Pablo, because he sets more aside every month
u1l1-9.explanation: What builds net worth is the gap between income and spending, not the salary.
feedback: No: what counts is the gap between what comes in and what goes out.
Marta only sets aside €50 a month: €3,000 in 5 years.
Pablo sets aside €300 a month: €18,000 in 5 years, six times more than Marta.

u1l2-1.prompt: With 3 % inflation for 20 years, how much will €1,000 buy in today's euros? (round it)
u1l2-1.explanation: 1,000 ÷ 1.03²⁰ ≈ €554. Every year prices rise and the same money buys less.

u1l2-2.explanation: It's 2 % in the medium term. That's why idle money loses value even in normal years.

u1l2-3.prompt: By the rule of 70, 2 % inflation halves purchasing power in about ____ years.

u1l2-4.prompt: What can push prices up? Tick all that apply.
options: The central bank raising rates sharply
A lot of money being created very quickly
Far more demand than there are products
u1l2-4.explanation: Raising rates is precisely how inflation is curbed: it makes credit dearer and cools demand.

u1l2-5.prompt: Match each situation with its effect on prices.
options: Everyone wants to buy at once
u1l2-5.explanation: Cost-push inflation, demand-pull inflation and the ECB's tool for curbing both.

u1l2-6.prompt: It's 2022: inflation in Spain hits 8 % and your account pays 0 %. You have €10,000 you won't need for 10 years. What do you do?
options: Look into options that at least aim to beat inflation in the long run
Nothing: money in the bank is safe
Spend it all before it's worth less
u1l2-6.explanation: Idle money isn't safe from inflation. Money you won't need for years should be put to work.
feedback: Good: over 10 years, leaving it idle is the surest way to lose purchasing power.
Your €10,000 buys 8 % less in a year: about €800 of purchasing power gone.
Spending out of fear doesn't protect your future: it just swaps saving for consumption.

u1l2-7.prompt: Quick: 7 % inflation. In how many years does your money buy half as much (rule of 70)?

u1l2-8.prompt: If prices fall across the board (deflation), it's always good news for the economy.
u1l2-8.explanation: Prolonged deflation makes people put off purchases and slows the economy; Japan suffered from it for years.

u1l2-9.prompt: What do you explain to Lumi?
options: That pesetas were worth more than euros
That money loses purchasing power to inflation year after year
That everything was just cheaper back then
u1l2-9.explanation: Inflation building up over decades means money buys less and less.
feedback: That's not it: €1 was worth 166.386 pesetas, but the problem is accumulated inflation.
Exactly! After decades of inflation, the same amount buys far fewer things.
Half true: what also changed was the value of money.
lines: My gran says that with 100 pesetas she could buy loads of stuff.

options: How much the prices of a consumer basket change
What a household earns on average
u1l3-1.explanation: It's a consumer price index: it compares the same basket over time.

u1l3-2.prompt: Is it included in core inflation?
u1l3-2.explanation: Core inflation leaves out energy and unprocessed food because they're the most volatile.

u1l3-3.prompt: Your personal inflation can differ from the official figure.
u1l3-3.explanation: The CPI weights items by average spending; your basket gives each thing a different weight.

u1l3-4.prompt: You rent, you drive everywhere, and petrol and rents have risen more than everything else. Official CPI is 3 %. What's most likely?
u1l3-4.explanation: If you spend more on what's rising most, your personal inflation beats the average.
feedback: Only if your basket looks like the average one, and yours doesn't.
Yes: you spend more on what has gone up most.
The prices you pay really have gone up.

u1l3-5.prompt: If electricity shoots up one month, headline CPI jumps a lot, but ____ inflation barely moves.
u1l3-5.explanation: Core inflation excludes energy to show the underlying trend.

u1l3-6.prompt: A basket cost €200 a year ago and costs €206 today. What has the inflation of that basket been?

u1l3-7.prompt: Match each profile with the part of the basket that affects them most.
u1l3-7.explanation: Every household has its own basket: that's why personal inflation varies.

u1l3-8.explanation: It leaves it out precisely because it's very volatile.

u1l3-9.prompt: What's true about the CPI? Tick all.
options: It compares prices with the same month the year before
Each product is weighted by average household spending
The INE publishes it every month
u1l3-9.explanation: The CPI is a weighted average of consumer prices.

u1l4-1.prompt: Your account pays 1.5 % and inflation is 2.7 %. What's your approximate real return?
u1l4-1.explanation: Real ≈ 1.5 − 2.7 = −1.2 %. You gain euros but lose purchasing power.

u1l4-2.prompt: If your account pays 3 % and inflation is 2 %, you gain purchasing power.

u1l4-3.prompt: Inflation at 2.5 %. Do you gain or lose purchasing power?
u1l4-3.explanation: You only gain if you earn more than inflation.

u1l4-4.prompt: What does the Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (Spain's deposit guarantee scheme) protect?
options: Up to €100,000 per person per bank if the bank goes bust
u1l4-4.explanation: It protects the euros you've deposited if the bank goes bust, not against inflation or stock market falls.

u1l4-5.prompt: You have €20,000 in an account paying 0 % and won't need it for 15 years. A friend says: «That way you don't lose anything». What do you say?
options: That I should put it all in a single share
He's right: the balance doesn't go down
That I lose purchasing power every year
u1l4-5.explanation: Money sitting still for years = lost purchasing power.
feedback: That's going from one extreme to the other: later on you'll see why to diversify.
The balance doesn't go down, but with 2.5 % inflation that €20,000 will buy what about €13,800 buys today in 15 years.
Exactly: you don't lose euros, you lose what you can buy with them.

u1l4-6.explanation: It's the quick way to tell whether your money is gaining or losing purchasing power.

u1l4-7.prompt: Quick: it earns 4 % and inflation is 3 %. Real return?

options: Safe, yes, but inflation eats away at their value bit by bit
Better take it out in cash
Yes, nothing happens to it there
feedback: Well spotted! Money you won't need soon can work to beat inflation.
In a drawer it loses to inflation just the same, and it can also get lost or stolen.
The euros are there, but every year they buy a bit less.
lines: I've had €5,000 in my current account for years.

u1l4-9.prompt: A guaranteed deposit can never make you lose purchasing power.
u1l4-9.explanation: If it earns less than inflation, you do lose it, even though the balance doesn't go down.

u1l5-1.prompt: €1,000 at 7 % compound interest for 30 years: what does it turn into? (round it)
u1l5-1.explanation: 1,000 × 1.07³⁰ ≈ €7,612. With simple interest it would be €3,100.

u1l5-2.prompt: Ana and Bruno each put in €200 a month at 7 %, but Ana starts 10 years earlier. At 65, Ana has…
u1l5-2.explanation: €524,963 versus €243,994: the early years are the ones that compound the most.

u1l5-3.prompt: Match each case with the type of interest.
options: You always earn on what you put in
You also earn on what you've already earned
A credit card debt that grows on itself
u1l5-3.explanation: Compounding speeds up growth… including the growth of debts.

u1l5-4.prompt: €10,000 at 5 % compound for 10 years: how much does it come to? (round to euros)
u1l5-4.explanation: 10,000 × 1.05¹⁰ ≈ €16,289. With simple interest it would be €15,000.

u1l5-5.prompt: Compound interest only works in your favour.
u1l5-5.explanation: It works against you too: a revolving credit card at 20 % doubles the debt in under 4 years.

u1l5-6.prompt: Put in order from lowest to highest the result of €100 a month for 30 years.
u1l5-6.explanation: €36,000, €49,273, €83,226 and €121,997: a few points of return make a huge difference to the end result.

u1l5-7.prompt: You're 22 and have €50 a month to invest. What do you do?
options: Spend it: €50 won't get you anywhere
Start now with €50 and raise the amount when I can
Wait until I earn more to start with something «serious»
u1l5-7.explanation: Starting early, even with a little, is what makes the most of compound interest.
feedback: €50 a month at 7 % for 40 years comes to about €130,000, with €24,000 put in.
Good: with time on your side, starting early matters more than starting big.
Waiting is costly: the early years are the ones with the most time to compound.

u1l5-8.prompt: With compound interest, money grows faster the more time passes.
u1l5-8.explanation: Each year you earn on a bigger base: the curve gets steeper over time.

u1l5-9.explanation: Each extra decade at 7 % almost doubles the money.
feedback: Time is exactly what matters most in compound interest.
Much more: 1,000 × 1.07⁴⁰ ≈ €14,974. The last 10 years almost double the result.
That's it! Ten more years at 7 % multiply it by almost 2 (1.07¹⁰ ≈ 1.97).
lines: I've seen that if I leave €1,000 at 7 %, in 30 years I'll have €7,600.
What if it's 40 years instead of 30?

u1l6-1.prompt: By the rule of 72, at 6 % a year money doubles in about ____ years.

u1l6-2.prompt: At 9 % a year, how many years does it take money to double according to the rule of 72?

u1l6-3.prompt: Quick: at 4 %, how many years to double?

u1l6-4.prompt: Match each return with the years it takes to double.

u1l6-5.prompt: A fund promises to double your money in 2 years «risk-free». What do you think?
options: I'll tell my family so they can invest too
I ask for details and stay suspicious
u1l6-5.explanation: The rule of 72 also helps you spot impossible promises.
feedback: Before dragging anyone in, do the maths: 72 ÷ 2 = 36 % a year. Too good to be true.
Good: a «risk-free» 36 % a year doesn't exist. Later you'll see how to check whether a firm is registered with the CNMV.
Doubling in 2 years needs 36 % a year (72 ÷ 2). Nobody offers that without risk: it's a classic scam sign.

u1l6-6.prompt: A revolving credit card charges 24 % a year. In how many years does the debt double if you don't pay?
u1l6-6.explanation: 72 ÷ 24 = 3 years. Compound interest also works for your creditor.

u1l6-7.prompt: The rule of 72 also works for inflation: at 3 %, prices double in about 24 years.

u1l6-8.prompt: To double your money in under 10 years, what return do you need?
u1l6-8.explanation: Under 10 years requires more than 7.2 % a year (72 ÷ 10).

options: Careful: it takes almost a third of your return and you take much longer to double
What matters is that the fund is well known
u1l6-9.explanation: Fees compound too: 2 % a year weighs a huge amount in the long run.
feedback: Exactly! 72 ÷ 7 ≈ 10 years versus 72 ÷ 5 ≈ 14 years.
Being well known doesn't reduce what it costs you each year.
After the fee you're left with 5 %: you double in ~14 years instead of ~10. Four years' difference.
lines: My fund returns 7 % but charges a 2 % fee a year.
